Cat breeds.Siamese: Siamese cats are famously vocal, with loud, almost human-sounding meows, and their dark points come from a heat-sensitive pigment.
Cat breeds.Persian: Persians are among the oldest recognized cat breeds, and their flat faces can cause breathing and tear-duct problems.
Cat breeds.Maine Coon: Maine Coons are among the largest domestic cats and are the official state cat of Maine, with tufted paws built for snow.
Cat breeds.Ragdoll: Ragdolls are named for tending to go limp when picked up, and they're large, docile cats with blue eyes.
Cat breeds.Sphynx: Sphynx cats look hairless but wear a fine down, and their skin needs regular baths because oils build up.
Cat breeds.Bengal: Bengals descend from crossing domestic cats with the wild Asian leopard cat, which gives them a spotted, rosetted coat.
Cat breeds.Abyssinian: Abyssinians are slender cats with 'ticked' fur, each hair banded in several colors; their true origin is uncertain despite the name.
Cat breeds.Burmese: Burmese cats trace back to a single cat, Wong Mau, brought from Burma to California in the 1930s.
Cat breeds.Russian Blue: Russian Blues have a dense, silvery-blue double coat and a gentle upturned mouth often called the 'Russian smile'.
Cat breeds.Scottish Fold: Scottish Folds get their folded ears from a cartilage mutation that can also cause painful joint problems, so breeding them is controversial.
Cat breeds.Manx: Manx cats have no tail or only a stub, a trait from a natural mutation on the Isle of Man.
Cat breeds.British Shorthair: British Shorthairs are stocky, round-faced cats, and the Cheshire Cat's grin is often linked to the breed.
Cat breeds.Pomeranian: Pomeranians are dogs, and the tiny ones descend from far larger sled-pulling Spitz dogs in Pomerania, now Poland and Germany.
Cat breeds.Shih Tzu: Shih Tzus are small Chinese palace dogs whose name means 'lion', and they're a dog breed, not a cat.
Cat breeds.Akita: Akitas are large Japanese dogs, and the famous Hachiko waited at a Tokyo station for his late owner for nearly ten years.
Cat breeds.Samoyed: Samoyeds are fluffy white dogs from Siberia, famous for a 'Sammy smile' because their mouth corners curl upward.
Cat breeds.Clydesdale: Clydesdales are heavy draft horses from Scotland, famous for feathered feet, so they aren't cats.
Cat breeds.Lhasa Apso: Lhasa Apsos are Tibetan dogs once kept as indoor sentinels in monasteries, which warned monks of strangers.
Cat breeds.Ocelot: Ocelots are wild cats of the Americas with striking spotted coats, but they're a species, not a domestic breed.
Cat breeds.Lynx: Lynx are wild cats with tufted ears and short tails; the Eurasian lynx is the largest of the group, but no breed of pet cat.
Cat breeds.Tabby: A tabby is a coat pattern of stripes, dots and the 'M' on the forehead, not a breed, and it appears in many breeds.
Cat breeds.Calico: Calico is a coat of white, orange and black patches, not a breed, and calicos are almost always female.
Cat breeds.Tortoiseshell: Tortoiseshell is a mottled black-and-orange coat found in many breeds, not a breed itself, and also almost always female.
Cat breeds.Weimaraner: Weimaraners are silvery-gray hunting dogs from Germany, nicknamed 'gray ghosts', so they're dogs, not cats.

Fruits that grow on trees.Apple: Apples float because about a quarter of their volume is air, and the thousands of varieties all trace back to wild apples from Kazakhstan.
Fruits that grow on trees.Pear: Pears ripen best off the tree, and growers pick them while still hard because they ripen from the core outward.
Fruits that grow on trees.Cherry: Cherry blossoms are celebrated each spring in Japan, and the fruit is a drupe, with a hard stone around the seed.
Fruits that grow on trees.Peach: Peaches belong to the same genus as plums and almonds, and nectarines are simply peaches with a smooth-skin gene.
Fruits that grow on trees.Plum: Plums dried become prunes, and the fruit comes in hundreds of varieties, from Japanese plums to European damsons.
Fruits that grow on trees.Orange: Oranges are a hybrid of pomelo and mandarin, and the color orange was named after the fruit, not the other way around.
Fruits that grow on trees.Lemon: Lemons are also a hybrid, probably of citron and bitter orange, and a lemon tree can bear fruit in all seasons.
Fruits that grow on trees.Mango: Mangoes are the national fruit of India, and a single tree can keep bearing fruit for over a hundred years.
Fruits that grow on trees.Avocado: Avocados are technically large berries with a single seed, and they grow on evergreen trees.
Fruits that grow on trees.Coconut: Coconuts grow on palm trees, which are tall woody plants, and a coconut can float for months before sprouting on a distant beach.
Fruits that grow on trees.Fig: Figs are not quite fruit: the fig is a flower-filled pod, and fig wasps pollinate it from the inside.
Fruits that grow on trees.Apricot: Apricots originated in Central Asia and China, and dried apricots are a classic food of Turkey, Iran and Armenia.
Fruits that grow on trees.Olive: Olives grow on trees that can live for well over a thousand years, and fresh from the branch they're far too bitter to eat.
Fruits that grow on trees.Strawberry: Strawberries grow on low plants, and they're the only fruit with its seeds on the outside, about 200 per berry.
Fruits that grow on trees.Blueberry: Blueberries grow on shrubs, not trees, and the dusty white bloom on them is a natural protective coating.
Fruits that grow on trees.Raspberry: Raspberries grow on prickly canes, and each berry is a cluster of tiny fruits called drupelets.
Fruits that grow on trees.Watermelon: Watermelons grow along the ground on vines and are about 92 percent water.
Fruits that grow on trees.Pineapple: Pineapples grow from the center of a low spiky plant on the ground, and each fruit takes well over a year to ripen.
Fruits that grow on trees.Grape: Grapes grow on vines, and over 70 percent of the world's harvest goes toward wine.
Fruits that grow on trees.Kiwi: Kiwifruit grows on vigorous vines, and it was once called Chinese gooseberry before being renamed after New Zealand's bird.
Fruits that grow on trees.Cranberry: Cranberries grow on low trailing vines in bogs and, since air pockets inside make them float, growers flood the bog to harvest.
Fruits that grow on trees.Blackberry: Blackberries grow on thorny canes, and each is an aggregate of many small fruitlets.
Fruits that grow on trees.Pumpkin: Pumpkins grow on sprawling vines on the ground, and they're a type of squash, technically a fruit.
Fruits that grow on trees.Passion fruit: Passion fruit grows on a climbing vine, and the name comes from missionaries who saw symbols of the Passion in its flower.

Rivers.Nile: Flowing north through Egypt for about 6,650 kilometers, it is traditionally counted the longest river in the world.
Rivers.Amazon: It carries more water than any other river, roughly a fifth of all the fresh water that flows into the oceans.
Rivers.Mississippi: Its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning great river; it drains parts of 31 US states.
Rivers.Yangtze: Asia's longest river, about 6,300 kilometers, runs through China and powers the giant Three Gorges Dam.
Rivers.Danube: It passes through ten countries, more than any other river on Earth, including four capital cities.
Rivers.Thames: London's river is tidal as far up as Teddington, and its name is among the oldest in Britain.
Rivers.Ganges: Sacred to Hindus, it flows from the Himalayas to the Bay of Bengal, and about 400 million people live in its basin.
Rivers.Rhine: A major European waterway from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea; Germany's Lorelei cliff lured sailors in legend.
Rivers.Volga: Europe's longest river, over 3,500 kilometers, runs entirely within Russia and is nicknamed Mother Volga.
Rivers.Mekong: Flowing through six countries from Tibet to Vietnam, its fishery feeds tens of millions, and it hosts giant freshwater catfish.
Rivers.Zambezi: Victoria Falls, called the smoke that thunders, sits on this African river, which is among the biggest on the continent.
Rivers.Seine: This river winds through Paris, where its banks are a UNESCO World Heritage site, and flows to the English Channel.
Rivers.Tigris: With the Euphrates it framed Mesopotamia, whose name means between rivers, the cradle of early cities and writing.
Rivers.Superior: A lake, not a river: Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area.
Rivers.Caspian: Called a sea but technically the world's largest lake, it is salty and has no ocean outlet.
Rivers.Baikal: A Siberian lake and the deepest on Earth, reaching about 1,600 meters, with seals found nowhere else.
Rivers.Titicaca: A lake on the Peru and Bolivia border and one of the highest large navigable lakes at about 3,800 meters.
Rivers.Mediterranean: A sea, not a river; its name means middle of the land, and it is almost entirely enclosed by continents.
Rivers.Erie: The shallowest of the Great Lakes is a lake, not a river, and it freezes over more often than the others.
Rivers.Tahoe: A deep, clear alpine lake straddling California and Nevada, not a river.
Rivers.Loch Ness: A Scottish lake, not a river, and it holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined.
Rivers.Dead Sea: A salt lake, not a river or sea, and its shore is the lowest dry land on Earth; salty water makes swimmers float.
Rivers.Suez Canal: A trap: it's a human-made channel that opened in 1869, not a natural river, linking the Mediterranean and Red seas.
Rivers.Panama Canal: A human-made waterway opened in 1914, not a river; ships are lifted by locks up to a lake.

Ice Age animals.Woolly mammoth: Frozen mammoths in Siberian permafrost have preserved fur, skin, and even stomach contents.
Ice Age animals.Smilodon: The saber-toothed cat's fangs reached about 18 centimeters, yet they were fragile, so it likely used them with care.
Ice Age animals.Woolly rhino: A shaggy rhino with a huge front horn, and its horn may have been used to sweep snow off plants.
Ice Age animals.Cave bear: Larger than most modern bears, it mostly ate plants, and thousands of its bones have been found in European caves.
Ice Age animals.Giant ground sloth: Some species like Megatherium were the size of elephants and walked on the sides of their feet.
Ice Age animals.Mastodon: A mastodon had low, flat-crowned teeth for browsing leaves and twigs, unlike the grazing teeth of mammoths.
Ice Age animals.Dire wolf: Heavier than the gray wolf, it hunted large prey in North America; its bones turned up by the hundreds in the La Brea tar pits.
Ice Age animals.Irish elk: It had the largest antlers of any deer ever, spanning up to about 3.5 meters, and its range extended far beyond Ireland.
Ice Age animals.Glyptodont: A giant armored relative of armadillos, as large as a small car, with a tail sometimes fitted with a spiked club.
Ice Age animals.Cave lion: Larger than modern lions, it appears in Ice Age cave art across Europe.
Ice Age animals.Short-faced bear: One of the largest meat-eating land mammals ever, it stood about 3.5 meters tall when on its hind legs.
Ice Age animals.Tyrannosaurus: A trap: dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago, long before the Ice Age began.
Ice Age animals.Triceratops: It lived in the late Cretaceous, tens of millions of years before any Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Stegosaurus: It lived in the Jurassic period, about 150 million years before the Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Pterodactyl: A flying reptile from the age of dinosaurs, which ended long before the Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Velociraptor: A small feathered dinosaur from about 75 million years ago, long before any Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Megalodon: This giant shark vanished about 3.6 million years ago, roughly before the Ice Age's big glaciations began.
Ice Age animals.Trilobite: An ancient sea creature that died out about 250 million years ago, long before the Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Dimetrodon: This sail-backed animal lived nearly 300 million years ago, ages before the Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Plesiosaur: A marine reptile of the dinosaur era, extinct about 66 million years ago.
Ice Age animals.Diplodocus: A long-necked dinosaur of the Jurassic, about 150 million years before the Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Spinosaurus: A Cretaceous giant that lived roughly 95 million years ago, far before the Ice Age.
Ice Age animals.Ammonite: A spiral-shelled sea creature that went extinct with the dinosaurs, and its fossils are common.
Ice Age animals.Archaeopteryx: A feathered, bird-like dinosaur from about 150 million years ago, ages before the Ice Age.

Countries bordering Germany.France: Germany's longest western neighbor along the Rhine; the two share a border town, Kehl, linked to Strasbourg by a bridge over the river.
Countries bordering Germany.Poland: Much of the border follows the Oder and Neisse rivers, fixed after World War II when Germany's eastern frontier moved west.
Countries bordering Germany.Austria: Shares a long southern border with Germany, and Bavaria and Austria speak related dialects, so the border is a cultural blur more than a line.
Countries bordering Germany.Switzerland: Germany and Switzerland meet along the Rhine and Lake Constance, where the exact border in the lake was never formally agreed.
Countries bordering Germany.Netherlands: The Dutch border is so porous that the town of Herzogenrath and Kerkrade share a street where the border runs down the middle.
Countries bordering Germany.Belgium: A short, quiet frontier in the Ardennes and Eifel; Belgium's small German-speaking community lives right along it.
Countries bordering Germany.Denmark: Germany's only land border in the north, and the only one with a Nordic country; each side has a recognized minority across it.
Countries bordering Germany.Czech Republic: Crossing the Ore Mountains, this border was once part of the Iron Curtain, and is now open under the Schengen agreement.
Countries bordering Germany.Luxembourg: Germany's smallest neighbor; the border follows the Moselle, where the Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 at the village of Schengen.
Countries bordering Germany.Italy: Close but no border: Austria and Switzerland sit between Germany and Italy, so the Alps are crossed twice.
Countries bordering Germany.Hungary: Hungary is a neighbor of Austria, not Germany, so Germany never touches it, a common trap.
Countries bordering Germany.Slovakia: Slovakia borders Austria, Czechia, Poland, Hungary and Ukraine, but not Germany; Czechia lies between.
Countries bordering Germany.Sweden: Sweden is across the Baltic Sea from Germany; they have maritime neighbors only, linked by ferries and the Öresund bridge nearby.
Countries bordering Germany.Norway: Norway has no land link to Germany; Denmark and the sea sit between them, and ferries connect Kiel and Oslo.
Countries bordering Germany.Spain: Spain is far to the southwest, with France in between, so Germany and Spain do not touch.
Countries bordering Germany.Slovenia: Slovenia borders Austria and Italy, not Germany; many people assume Alpine neighbors all touch Germany, but they don't.
Countries bordering Germany.Liechtenstein: Tiny and doubly landlocked, Liechtenstein only touches Switzerland and Austria, not Germany, despite its German language.
Countries bordering Germany.Lithuania: Lithuania is on the Baltic, but Poland and Russia's Kaliningrad lie between it and Germany.
Countries bordering Germany.UK: The UK is separated from Germany by the North Sea and the Channel; its only land border is with Ireland.
Countries bordering Germany.Croatia: Croatia touches Slovenia, Hungary, Serbia, Bosnia and Montenegro, but no German-speaking country, so Germany is not a neighbor.
Countries bordering Germany.Finland: Finland borders Sweden, Norway and Russia, and reaches Germany only across the Baltic Sea.
Countries bordering Germany.Portugal: Portugal's only land neighbor is Spain, so it's among the farthest from Germany.
Countries bordering Germany.Belarus: Belarus sits two countries east of Germany, behind Poland, so they share no border.
Countries bordering Germany.Ukraine: Europe's largest country wholly within the continent, but Poland and Slovakia lie between it and Germany, so there's no shared border.

Countries in Europe.Portugal: The oldest fixed borders in Europe date to 1297, and its alliance with England, from 1386, is among the oldest in the world.
Countries in Europe.Belgium: It has three official languages, Dutch, French, and German, and it has gone through periods without a formal government for over 500 days.
Countries in Europe.Slovenia: Tiny but green, with the Julian Alps, the Postojna caves, and forest covering over half its land.
Countries in Europe.Estonia: The country is a digital pioneer, with online voting since 2005 and the invention of Skype.
Countries in Europe.Moldova: It holds the biggest wine cellar in the world, Milestii Mici, with underground tunnels of about 200 kilometers.
Countries in Europe.Albania: Its name for itself is Shqiperia, 'land of the eagles', and it has hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers from the Hoxha era.
Countries in Europe.Iceland: It has no army and no mosquitoes, and its parliament, the Althing, dates to 930.
Countries in Europe.Malta: This tiny island country is one of the world's most densely populated, and the Knights of St John built its capital, Valletta.
Countries in Europe.Luxembourg: One of the world's richest countries per person, with three official languages and the world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy.
Countries in Europe.Liechtenstein: It is one of two doubly landlocked countries, and Switzerland's franc is its currency.
Countries in Europe.Andorra: It has two co-princes, the president of France and a Spanish bishop, and it sits high in the Pyrenees.
Countries in Europe.Serbia: Nikola Tesla was born to a Serb family in a village in what is now Croatia, and the country is a leading raspberry producer.
Countries in Europe.Lithuania: It was the last pagan country in Europe, converting to Christianity only in 1387.
Countries in Europe.Tunisia: Trap: it is in North Africa, even though ancient Carthage was just a short sail from Sicily.
Countries in Europe.Morocco: Trap: Africa, only about 13 kilometers from Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar.
Countries in Europe.Israel: Trap: in Western Asia, though it competes in European sports bodies like UEFA and the Eurovision Song Contest.
Countries in Europe.Lebanon: Trap: a Middle Eastern country on the Mediterranean, and it features a cedar tree on its flag.
Countries in Europe.Iran: Trap: a Western Asian country, whose old name Persia ruled lands bordering Europe.
Countries in Europe.Libya: Trap: a North African country, and most of it is the Sahara.
Countries in Europe.Mongolia: Trap: an Asian country, and its distance to Europe is vast, but Genghis Khan's empire reached eastern Europe.
Countries in Europe.Uruguay: Trap: a South American country, and it hosted and won the first soccer World Cup in 1930.
Countries in Europe.Jordan: Trap: a Middle Eastern country with Petra, the rose-red city carved in rock.
Countries in Europe.Algeria: Trap: Africa's largest country by area, and it sits across the Mediterranean from Europe.
Countries in Europe.Syria: Trap: a Middle Eastern country with Damascus, among the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities.

Body parts found in birds.Beak: Beaks are made of bone covered by keratin, the same material as your fingernails. Their shapes reflect diets, from seed cracking to nectar sipping.
Body parts found in birds.Talons: Eagles and owls have powerful talons for gripping prey. An eagle's grip can be several times stronger than a human hand's.
Body parts found in birds.Feathers: Feathers are the one thing that only birds have among living animals. A swan can have around 25,000 of them.
Body parts found in birds.Gizzard: A muscular stomach that grinds food, since birds have no teeth. Many birds swallow small stones to help the grinding.
Body parts found in birds.Crop: A pouch in the throat for storing food. Pigeons use theirs to make crop milk, a nutritious fluid that feeds their chicks.
Body parts found in birds.Wishbone: The wishbone is actually two fused collarbones. It acts as a spring that stores energy as the wings beat.
Body parts found in birds.Syrinx: The bird's voice box, found deep at the base of the windpipe. Songbirds can control each side separately and sing two notes at once.
Body parts found in birds.Keel: A ridge on the breastbone, anchoring the large flight muscles. Flightless birds like ostriches lack it.
Body parts found in birds.Air sacs: Birds have air sacs that make their lungs one-way, giving oxygen both when they inhale and exhale. This helps them fly at altitudes where we'd faint.
Body parts found in birds.Hollow bones: Many bird bones contain air spaces connected to the respiratory system. A frigatebird's skeleton can weigh less than its feathers.
Body parts found in birds.Teeth: Modern birds have no teeth. Their ancient ancestors had them, and chicks carry a tiny egg tooth to break out of the shell.
Body parts found in birds.Gills: Gills are for breathing underwater. Birds, including penguins, breathe air with lungs.
Body parts found in birds.Fins: Fins belong to fish. Penguins use their wings as flippers, but those are still wings.
Body parts found in birds.Udder: Mammals like cows have udders. Birds don't produce milk, though pigeons make a milk-like crop secretion.
Body parts found in birds.Antlers: Antlers are grown by deer, and are shed and regrown yearly. Birds grow no such bony structures, though some have horn-like casques.
Body parts found in birds.Whiskers: Whiskers are for mammals. Some birds have bristle-like feathers around the beak that do a similar sensing job.
Body parts found in birds.Mane: A mane belongs to lions and horses. Birds have feathered crests, not manes.
Body parts found in birds.Tusks: Tusks are very long teeth, found in elephants and walruses. Birds have no teeth at all.
Body parts found in birds.Diaphragm: Mammals use this muscle to breathe. Birds have no true diaphragm, and move air by using their rib and breast muscles.
Body parts found in birds.Sweat glands: Birds have virtually none. They cool off by panting, or by fluttering the skin at their throat.
Body parts found in birds.Fur: Fur is a mammal trait. Birds have feathers, which evolved from the same ancestors as dinosaurs' scales.
Body parts found in birds.Blowhole: A blowhole lets whales and dolphins breathe at the surface. Birds breathe through nostrils on the beak.
Body parts found in birds.Tentacles: Tentacles are found in squids and octopuses. Birds have wings, legs and a beak, but no tentacles.
Body parts found in birds.Pouch: Marsupials carry young in a pouch. Pelicans have a throat pouch, but that's a feature of the bill, not a baby carrier.

Percussion instruments.Snare drum: The wires, called snares, stretched under the lower head give the drum its crisp rattle, and they can be switched off.
Percussion instruments.Timpani: Orchestral kettledrums can be tuned to specific pitches with pedals, so unlike most drums they play real melodies.
Percussion instruments.Xylophone: Its name comes from Greek for 'wood sound', and its wooden bars are struck by mallets, with a bright, dry tone.
Percussion instruments.Triangle: A bent steel bar struck with a beater, the triangle can cut through a whole orchestra despite its tiny size.
Percussion instruments.Cymbal: Turkish makers such as Zildjian, a family business that began in Istanbul in 1623, have long made the best cymbals.
Percussion instruments.Tambourine: Small metal jingles set in a frame give the tambourine its shimmer, and it has been played since ancient times.
Percussion instruments.Maracas: A pair of rattles filled with seeds or beads, they come from the Americas, and are used in Latin music.
Percussion instruments.Bongo: These small paired hand drums came from Cuba, where they became central to son and salsa music.
Percussion instruments.Glockenspiel: The name is German for 'bell play', and Mozart's The Magic Flute has a part for it, with metal bars struck by mallets.
Percussion instruments.Castanets: Clicking wooden shells held in the hand, associated with Spanish flamenco, though their roots are far older.
Percussion instruments.Cowbell: Originally a bell hung from livestock, it became famous through the Saturday Night Live 'more cowbell' sketch.
Percussion instruments.Marimba: A bigger, deeper relative of the xylophone, with resonator tubes under its wooden bars, and it's a national instrument of Guatemala.
Percussion instruments.Gong: A hanging metal disc struck with a mallet, it has been used in Southeast Asian music for centuries.
Percussion instruments.Djembe: A goblet-shaped hand drum from West Africa, traditionally carved from a single piece of wood, with a goatskin head.
Percussion instruments.Trumpet: A brass instrument whose sound comes from buzzing lips, and its player blows it rather than striking it.
Percussion instruments.Flute: A woodwind played by blowing across a hole, and nothing is struck, so it is not percussion.
Percussion instruments.Harp: Its strings are plucked, so it belongs to the string family rather than percussion, though it is often placed near the percussion in orchestras.
Percussion instruments.Cello: A bowed string instrument, so it isn't percussion, though players sometimes tap the strings with the bow's wood, in a technique called col legno.
Percussion instruments.Oboe: A double-reed woodwind, so it is blown rather than struck, and its piercing tone is the pitch the orchestra tunes to.
Percussion instruments.Banjo: Its round, drum-like head looks like percussion, but the sound is from plucked strings, so it is a string instrument.
Percussion instruments.Harmonica: A free-reed wind instrument, whose sound comes from air passing across metal reeds, so it is not struck.
Percussion instruments.Accordion: Squeezed bellows push air over reeds, so it is a free-reed instrument and not percussion, despite its rhythmic role in folk music.
Percussion instruments.Bagpipes: They sound by air from a bag across reeds, so they are wind instruments and nothing is struck.
Percussion instruments.Sitar: An Indian plucked string instrument with sympathetic strings, so it sits in the string family, not percussion.

Rolling Stones songs.Satisfaction: Keith Richards dreamed the fuzzy riff, half-woke and recorded it on a cassette. The 1965 single gave the Stones their first US number one.
Rolling Stones songs.Paint It Black: Brian Jones's droning sitar gave this 1966 chart-topper its eerie sound, a rare instrument in rock at the time.
Rolling Stones songs.Angie: This 1973 ballad was long rumored to be about David Bowie's wife, but Keith Richards says it was named for his baby daughter, Dandelion Angela.
Rolling Stones songs.Brown Sugar: Recorded at Muscle Shoals in 1969 and a US number one in 1971, it was later dropped from the band's live sets because of its lyrics about slavery.
Rolling Stones songs.Start Me Up: It began life as a reggae-tinged demo that sat unused for years. Microsoft later licensed the 1981 rocker to launch Windows 95.
Rolling Stones songs.Wild Horses: Gram Parsons's band, the Flying Burrito Brothers, released a version before the Stones did. The aching 1971 ballad was recorded at Muscle Shoals.
Rolling Stones songs.Gimme Shelter: Guest singer Merry Clayton belted the famous cracking vocal after being called out of bed late at night. It opens the 1969 album Let It Bleed.
Rolling Stones songs.Miss You: Their 1978 US number one borrowed a disco pulse, proving the band could ride the dance craze that was sweeping the clubs.
Rolling Stones songs.Ruby Tuesday: Brian Jones played the recorder on this 1967 ballad, which hit number one in the US as the flip side of Let's Spend the Night Together.
Rolling Stones songs.Jumpin' Jack Flash: The title came from Keith Richards's gardener, Jack Dyer, who stomped past the window one rainy morning. The riff uses open tuning.
Rolling Stones songs.Honky Tonk Women: The 1969 number one opens with a lone cowbell. Its country-flavored cousin, Country Honk, appears on the album Let It Bleed.
Rolling Stones songs.Hey Jude: A Beatles song, not a Stones one. At over seven minutes, it was the longest number one single of its era in 1968.
Rolling Stones songs.Layla: Eric Clapton wrote it for Pattie Boyd, wife of his friend George Harrison, borrowing the name from a Persian love poem.
Rolling Stones songs.Stairway to Heaven: Led Zeppelin never released this as a single, yet it became one of the most requested songs in rock radio history.
Rolling Stones songs.Purple Haze: Jimi Hendrix's 1967 debut-era classic, built on a tritone riff once called the devil's interval, has nothing to do with the Stones.
Rolling Stones songs.Light My Fire: A Doors hit from 1967. Guitarist Robby Krieger wrote most of it, and Ray Manzarek's organ solo drives it.
Rolling Stones songs.Smoke on the Water: Deep Purple wrote it about a real fire at the Montreux casino during a Frank Zappa concert. Its riff is every beginner guitarist's first lesson.
Rolling Stones songs.Back in Black: AC/DC's tribute to singer Bon Scott, who had just died. The 1980 album is among the best-selling ever made.
Rolling Stones songs.My Generation: The Who's 1965 anthem has the line 'Hope I die before I get old', delivered with a stutter meant to sound like a pill-popping mod.
Rolling Stones songs.Born to Run: Bruce Springsteen's 1975 breakthrough landed him on the covers of both Time and Newsweek in the same week.
Rolling Stones songs.Come Together: A Beatles opener on Abbey Road. Chuck Berry's publisher sued because one line echoed his song You Can't Catch Me.
Rolling Stones songs.Hotel California: The Eagles' 1977 epic won Record of the Year. Its closing guitar duel between Don Felder and Joe Walsh is among rock's most famous.
Rolling Stones songs.Sweet Child o' Mine: Slash was only noodling on a warm-up exercise when the riff was born. This Guns N' Roses 1987 song became their only US number one.
Rolling Stones songs.Let It Be: Paul McCartney said the lyric came from a dream of his late mother, Mary, who told him 'let it be'. It is a Beatles song.

Bands with an animal in their name.Arctic Monkeys: This Sheffield band's 2006 debut became the fastest-selling debut album in UK chart history at that time.
Bands with an animal in their name.Eagles: The Eagles' 'Their Greatest Hits 1971-1975' became one of the best-selling albums ever in the US.
Bands with an animal in their name.Counting Crows: The band took its name from an old rhyme that predicts the future from the number of crows seen.
Bands with an animal in their name.Whitesnake: David Coverdale named the band after his 1977 solo album, formed after leaving Deep Purple, and it later topped charts with 'Here I Go Again'.
Bands with an animal in their name.Cage the Elephant: The Kentucky band's name came from a rant by a stranger who told the singer's brother to cage the elephant.
Bands with an animal in their name.Iron Butterfly: Iron Butterfly's 17-minute 'In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida' helped invent the long, heavy rock song.

Instruments that use a reed.Clarinet: Its single reed vibrates against the mouthpiece. Mozart wrote a famous concerto for it, which helped make it a standard orchestral instrument.
Instruments that use a reed.Oboe: It uses a double reed, and the orchestra tunes to its A. Players often make their own reeds by hand.
Instruments that use a reed.Bassoon: It has a double reed and nearly 9 feet of tubing, folded in half. It is among the longest wind instruments.
Instruments that use a reed.Saxophone: Adolphe Sax patented it in the 1840s. Though made of brass, it is a woodwind because of its single reed.
Instruments that use a reed.Harmonica: Tiny metal reeds inside vibrate as you blow or draw air through the holes. It is small enough to fit in a pocket.
Instruments that use a reed.Accordion: Bellows push air across metal reeds. Its ancestor, the Chinese sheng, uses free reeds, and so does the modern accordion.
Instruments that use a reed.Bagpipes: The drone pipes and chanter use reeds, fed by air from a bag. The Highland pipes are built around a continuous sound.
Instruments that use a reed.English horn: It is neither English nor a horn. It is a double-reed oboe pitched lower, and the name's origin is still debated.
Instruments that use a reed.Melodica: Blow into a mouthpiece and play a small keyboard that drives metal reeds. It is used in schools and by dub and jazz artists.
Instruments that use a reed.Harmonium: A pump organ with free metal reeds. It is central to Indian devotional singing, though it originated in 19th-century Paris.
Instruments that use a reed.Contrabassoon: It reaches an octave below the bassoon, with about 16 feet of tube. Its tone is a deep rumble.
Instruments that use a reed.Flute: There is no reed: players blow across a hole, as with a bottle. Modern concert flutes are metal, though they count as woodwinds.
Instruments that use a reed.Piccolo: It is a small flute and so has no reed. It is the highest-pitched instrument in a standard orchestra.
Instruments that use a reed.Recorder: The recorder's air is shaped by a fipple edge, not a reed. Samuel Pepys wrote about playing it in the 1600s.
Instruments that use a reed.Pan flute: Panpipes are blown across the tops of tubes with no reed. They're named for the Greek god Pan.
Instruments that use a reed.Ocarina: A clay or ceramic whistle with finger holes, with no reed. Its name is Italian for little goose.
Instruments that use a reed.Tin whistle: A simple fipple flute, popular in Irish music, with no reed. It's also called a penny whistle.
Instruments that use a reed.Trumpet: Brass players buzz their lips into a cup mouthpiece instead of using a reed. Trumpets date back thousands of years.
Instruments that use a reed.Trombone: A slide changes the pitch, and the buzzing lips do the work, so no reed. Its name in Italian means big trumpet.
Instruments that use a reed.Tuba: This is the largest brass instrument, played with lips and no reed. It can contain about 18 feet of tubing.
Instruments that use a reed.French horn: Brass, buzzed with the lips. It has some 12 feet of coiled tubing, and the player's hand in the bell adjusts tone.
Instruments that use a reed.Kazoo: A kazoo uses a membrane that buzzes with your voice, not a reed. It's often credited to 19th-century America.
Instruments that use a reed.Didgeridoo: Indigenous Australians play it by buzzing the lips into a hollowed wooden tube. Circular breathing keeps the drone going.
Instruments that use a reed.Fife: A small high-pitched flute used in military bands and fife-and-drum corps. It has no reed.

Places in Greek mythology.Elysium: The afterlife paradise for heroes and the virtuous; its name lives on as the Champs-Elysees in Paris.
Places in Greek mythology.River Styx: The river the gods swore their most solemn oaths upon; breaking such an oath meant a year of silence.
Places in Greek mythology.Troy: The city of the Trojan War, which really existed: its ruins at Hisarlik in Turkey were identified in the 1870s.
Places in Greek mythology.Ithaca: Odysseus's island home is a real Greek island, though which one Homer meant has been debated.
Places in Greek mythology.Delphi: Site of Apollo's oracle, where the priestess Pythia gave prophecies; the Greeks thought it was the center of the world.
Places in Greek mythology.Labyrinth: The maze built by Daedalus for the Minotaur; the double-headed axe, labrys, may give its name.
Places in Greek mythology.Lethe: The river of forgetfulness in Hades; the dead who drank from it lost all memory of life.
Places in Greek mythology.Asphodel Meadows: The grey, ordinary afterlife where most souls went, those who were neither great nor wicked.
Places in Greek mythology.Colchis: The kingdom of the Golden Fleece, based on the real region on the east of the Black Sea, in today's Georgia.
Places in Greek mythology.Erebus: The dark, shadowy part of the underworld, also the name of a primordial god of darkness.
Places in Greek mythology.Asgard: A trap: this is the Norse gods' realm, linked to the rainbow bridge, and not part of Greek myth.
Places in Greek mythology.Valhalla: A trap: Odin's hall where slain warriors feast is Norse, nothing to do with Greek afterlives like Elysium.
Places in Greek mythology.Midgard: A trap: it's the Norse world of humans, and its name is the root of Tolkien's Middle-earth.
Places in Greek mythology.Avalon: A trap: the island where Arthur was taken to heal is British legend, not Greek myth.
Places in Greek mythology.Camelot: A trap: Arthur's court belongs to British legend, not to the Greek world of Olympus and Troy.
Places in Greek mythology.Lilliput: A trap: Jonathan Swift invented this island of six-inch people for 'Gulliver's Travels' in 1726.
Places in Greek mythology.Shangri-La: A trap: James Hilton's fictional Himalayan paradise, from his 1933 novel 'Lost Horizon'.
Places in Greek mythology.El Dorado: A trap: the Spanish legend of a golden city or king, born in South America in the 1500s, not Greek.
Places in Greek mythology.Narnia: C. S. Lewis's fantasy world, begun with 'The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe' in 1950.

Places in Greek mythology.Neverland: A trap: J. M. Barrie's island of Peter Pan first appeared in his 1904 play, not Greek myth.

Historic African kingdoms and empires.Songhai: A 15th and 16th century West African empire, bigger than Mali at its peak, with Timbuktu and Gao as great centres of learning and trade.
Historic African kingdoms and empires.Great Zimbabwe: A stone-walled city in modern Zimbabwe, built from about 1100. The country took its name from it, and its walls use no mortar.
Historic African kingdoms and empires.Carthage: A Phoenician city in modern Tunisia, famed for Hannibal, who crossed the Alps with elephants. Rome destroyed it in 146 BC.

Historic African kingdoms and empires.Kongo: A Central African kingdom at the mouth of the Congo, which exchanged ambassadors with Portugal and whose king converted to Christianity in 1491.
Historic African kingdoms and empires.Zulu Kingdom: Shaka Zulu forged it in the 1810s from smaller clans, using short stabbing spears and disciplined regiments. It later defeated a British force at Isandlwana in 1879.

Things with a lid.Jar: Canning jars rely on a lid that seals as the contents cool, and the little pop you hear is the vacuum forming.
Things with a lid.Toilet: Many countries now ask people to close the lid before flushing, because a flush can spray a fine mist of droplets into the air.
Things with a lid.Laptop: Closing the lid usually triggers sleep mode via a small magnet sensor, so you can end a session without pressing any button.
Things with a lid.Teapot: Teapot lids often have a tiny hole to let steam escape, which also keeps the tea from dripping when you pour.
Things with a lid.Trash can: Pedal-operated lids were popularized by early 1900s hospital designs, so a nurse could keep both hands free and clean.
Things with a lid.Shoebox: A cardboard shoebox lid sits loose over the box, and shoeboxes have a long second life as diorama and keepsake storage.
Things with a lid.Thermos: The vacuum flask was invented around 1892 by James Dewar, who used it for science, and its lid is often the cup too.
Things with a lid.Kettle: Kettle lids often have a tight fit so steam can build pressure, and some designs lock to prevent a scalding spill.
Things with a lid.Food container: Many containers have vented lids to prevent a vacuum in the microwave, and the lid is where the recycling code often sits.
Things with a lid.Paint can: The rim groove holds a little paint, so the lid must be pried with a flat tool and tapped shut with a hammer for a proper seal.
Things with a lid.Treasure chest: Real pirate treasure chests were rare, and no verified buried treasure map marked with an X exists; that image came from fiction.
Things with a lid.Plate: A plate is open and flat, with no lid. Plates have been made of everything from wood to gold, but they stay lidless.
Things with a lid.Fork: Forks have no lid, just tines. Forks spread in Europe slowly, and some church leaders once saw them as an affront to God.
Things with a lid.Spoon: No lid here. Spoons are among the oldest utensils, and the earliest ones were carved from wood, bone, and shells.
Things with a lid.Cutting board: It is a flat slab with no lid. Wooden boards are generally considered as hygienic as plastic ones when kept clean.
Things with a lid.Spatula: A spatula has no lid; the lid in the kitchen belongs to the pot, not the tool that flips what's in it.
Things with a lid.Ladder: A ladder has rungs and rails, not a lid. The oldest known ladder images date back about 10,000 years in cave art.
Things with a lid.Towel: No lid, only fabric. Terry cloth towels get their absorbency from thousands of tiny loops of cotton thread.
Things with a lid.Broom: A broom has bristles, not a lid. Witches' flying brooms come from folklore, long before the cartoon image.
Things with a lid.Mirror: No lid here, even though a hand mirror sometimes comes in a compact case that does have one.
Things with a lid.Candle: Candles have no lid, although some jar candles come with one to keep dust off and the scent in.
Things with a lid.Chair: A chair has a seat and a back, and no lid, unlike the bin or box you might sit on in a pinch.
Things with a lid.Rug: A rug lies flat on the floor with no lid. Some hand-knotted rugs take a weaver months or years to finish.

Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Takeout menu: Takeout menus pile up in drawers because people save them for the next time they feel lazy about dinner.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Spare key: The spare key is a classic junk drawer resident, though nobody remembers which lock it opens.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Sticky tape: Clear tape was invented by Richard Drew of 3M in 1930, and it still seems to disappear when you need it.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Pens: Drawers often hold pens that no longer write, because people keep them 'just in case'.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Birthday candles: Birthday candles in the drawer are the stubs of past celebrations, saved for a future cake.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Twist ties: Twist ties are a thin wire inside paper or plastic, and they hold bread bags shut.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Matches: Safety matches were invented in Sweden in the 1840s, and they only light when struck on the special strip.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Old phone charger: Old chargers pile up because every new phone seems to need a different cable.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Coupons: Coupons in junk drawers tend to expire before they are used.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Paper clips: Paper clips are small, cheap and useful, and they are in nearly every junk drawer, for resetting gadgets as well.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Takeout chopsticks: Free chopsticks from takeout orders collect in drawers, even if nobody in the house uses them.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Frozen peas: Frozen peas would thaw in a drawer, so they belong in the freezer.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Milk: Milk spoils quickly at room temperature, so it belongs in the fridge, not in a drawer.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Raw eggs: Raw eggs need refrigeration in the US, and a drawer is no place to keep them.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Goldfish: A goldfish needs water, and a junk drawer has none.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Houseplant: Plants need light and water, and a closed drawer offers neither.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Wedding cake: A wedding cake is far too big and fragile for a drawer.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Live lobster: A live lobster belongs in a tank or on ice, certainly not in a drawer.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Ice cream: Ice cream would melt into a puddle in a drawer.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Bathtub: A bathtub is a fixed fixture, far too big for any drawer.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Lawnmower: A lawnmower is large and belongs in the garage, not a kitchen drawer.
Things you'd find in a junk drawer.Sofa: A sofa is a large piece of furniture, much too big for a drawer.

Parts of a bed.Headboard: A headboard often serves as a back support, and the earliest ones were designed to keep out cold drafts from walls.
Parts of a bed.Footboard: A footboard sits at the foot end and in the past it kept the bedding from sliding off.
Parts of a bed.Mattress: The mattress is the star of the bed, and people spend about a third of their lives on one.
Parts of a bed.Box spring: A box spring was once built with real coils to add bounce, but many today are just a rigid wood frame.
Parts of a bed.Bed frame: A bed frame supports the mattress and can be made of wood, metal or upholstered material.
Parts of a bed.Slats: Slats support the mattress and let it breathe, replacing a box spring in many beds.
Parts of a bed.Valance: A valance is a decorative skirt that hides the space under the bed, and it hides what's under the bed too.
Parts of a bed.Canopy: A canopy hangs over a four-poster bed, and it once kept off drafts and insects.
Parts of a bed.Bed rail: A bed rail stops small children from rolling out of bed, and also helps older people get up.
Parts of a bed.Lampshade: A lampshade softens a lamp's light and hides the bare bulb, and has no role in holding up a bed.
Parts of a bed.Armrest: An armrest is part of a chair or sofa, where it supports the arm; a bed has no need for one.
Parts of a bed.Pedal: A pedal is pushed by the foot on a bike, piano or car, and it makes no sense on a bed.
Parts of a bed.Doorknob: A doorknob is a door's handle, and the round version we know today took off in the 1800s.
Parts of a bed.Tabletop: A tabletop is the flat surface of a table, and early ones were just planks laid across trestles.
Parts of a bed.Backrest: A backrest supports the back of a chair, although a bed's headboard does much the same job when you sit up to read.
Parts of a bed.Spout: A spout is the pouring part of a kettle or jug, and the word is old enough to come from Middle English.
Parts of a bed.Wick: A wick is the cord in a candle that draws melted wax up to burn, and has nothing to do with sleeping.
Parts of a bed.Lid: A lid covers a pot or jar, while a bed is left open for you to climb into.
Parts of a bed.Faucet: A faucet is plumbing, and the word is American for what the British call a tap.
Parts of a bed.Keyhole: A keyhole belongs to a door lock, and it's one hole nobody wants in a bed.
Parts of a bed.Plug: A plug seals a sink or connects an appliance to the mains, and a bed has neither job.
Parts of a bed.Dial: A dial belongs to a clock, radio or phone; the word comes from the Latin for day, dies, because sundials marked days.
Parts of a bed.Antenna: An antenna belongs to a radio or TV, and insects have them too, to smell and feel the world.
Parts of a bed.Seat cushion: A seat cushion sits on a chair or sofa, and a mattress does the same work for a bed on a bigger scale.

Things to hide from a toddler.Scissors: Scissors are a classic hazard because toddlers love to copy grown-ups; safety scissors with rounded tips are made for little hands.
Things to hide from a toddler.Matches: Matches are a fire risk, and toddlers imitate adults striking them; fire experts say to keep them locked away.
Things to hide from a toddler.Permanent marker: Permanent marker works on walls, skin and furniture, and its fumes and its stains are tough to clean up.
Things to hide from a toddler.Glitter: Glitter spreads everywhere and gets into eyes and mouths; it was once metal flakes, and today's is plastic.
Things to hide from a toddler.Medicine: Medicine can look like candy, and accidental poisoning in young children is common; child-proof caps only slow them down.
Things to hide from a toddler.Kitchen knife: Kitchen knives belong out of reach; toddlers can climb and grab, so a locked drawer helps.
Things to hide from a toddler.Bleach: Bleach is a toxic cleaner that can burn skin and mouth, and mixing it with ammonia produces poisonous gas.
Things to hide from a toddler.Lighter: Lighters are easy to flick; US safety rules require child-resistant ones since 1994, though toddlers still can work them.
Things to hide from a toddler.Superglue: Superglue bonds skin in seconds; it was discovered by accident in the 1940s, and was first thought a failure.
Things to hide from a toddler.Button batteries: Button batteries are among the most dangerous swallowed objects; stuck in the throat they can burn through tissue in hours.
Things to hide from a toddler.Nail polish: Nail polish contains solvents that are harmful if swallowed or inhaled, and the bright bottles are enticing.
Things to hide from a toddler.Marbles: Marbles are a choking hazard; anything small enough to fit through a toilet-paper tube is too small for toddlers.
Things to hide from a toddler.Board book: A trap: board books are made to be chewed and thrown, with thick cardboard pages that stand up to toddler abuse.
Things to hide from a toddler.Stuffed bunny: Stuffed bunnies are safe, if the eyes are embroidered rather than loose buttons; they're a classic comfort item.
Things to hide from a toddler.Wooden blocks: Wooden blocks are classic toys that build coordination, and large ones are safe as they can't be swallowed.
Things to hide from a toddler.Sippy cup: A sippy cup is designed for spill-free, safe drinking and doesn't need to be hidden.
Things to hide from a toddler.Rattle: A rattle is among the oldest baby toys; archaeologists have found them in ancient Roman and Egyptian sites.
Things to hide from a toddler.Rubber duck: Rubber ducks are bath-time staples; as ones from a 1992 spill in the Pacific showed, they float for years.
Things to hide from a toddler.Teething ring: A teething ring is made to be chewed and soothe sore gums, and often comes chilled.
Things to hide from a toddler.Picture book: Picture books are fine for toddlers and help vocabulary; reading to children builds language from early infancy.
Things to hide from a toddler.Soft ball: A soft ball is safe to throw indoors, and large soft balls can't be swallowed or break anything.
Things to hide from a toddler.Baby blanket: A baby blanket is safe when awake, though experts say to keep loose bedding out of a sleeping infant's crib.
Things to hide from a toddler.Stacking cups: Stacking cups teach size and balance and are too big to swallow, so they're safe.
Things to hide from a toddler.Pacifier: A pacifier is made for babies to suck on, with a vented shield so it's safe if it goes in the mouth.

Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Bacon: Grease would leave a permanent stain on the pages, and bacon's smell would tempt every pet in the house.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Slice of cheese: Cheese would sweat oil into the paper and attract mold; a book would smell odd for years.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Spaghetti: Cooked spaghetti would turn into a limp, sticky smear, and there's no way a noodle holds a page.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Banana peel: A banana peel is slippery, mushy and quick to brown, so it would stain your pages in hours.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Lit match: A lit match would burn the book, and paper ignites at about 451 degrees Fahrenheit, the number in the title of Fahrenheit 451.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Wet noodle: A wet noodle is a limp, soggy mess, and the phrase 'wet noodle' means someone weak or ineffectual.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Pancake: A pancake is greasy, floppy and sticky with syrup, so it's a doomed bookmark.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Jam sandwich: Jam would glue the pages together, and a sandwich would add crumbs and grease.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Ice cube: An ice cube melts in minutes, and the water would warp and wrinkle the paper.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Fried egg: Fried egg yolk would stain and stick, and it's both greasy and runny.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Sardine: Sardines come in oil, and the fishy smell would haunt the pages forever.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Ribbon: A ribbon is often built into the book itself, and hardcovers often include a sewn-in ribbon marker.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Receipt: Receipts are the classic, pocket-sized scrap, though thermal paper ones can fade over time.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Postcard: Postcards are sturdy, and stiff enough to hold a place, and doubly nice if from a place you've been.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Ticket stub: A ticket stub keeps both your place and a memory, which is why people save them in books.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Pressed flower: Pressed flowers go back to Victorian times, though a wet bloom would stain the page.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Playing card: A playing card is stiff and sturdy and the right size for a paperback, a handy substitute.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Paper clip: Paper clips date from the 1890s, and they hold a page but can dent or rust the paper over time.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Bus ticket: A bus ticket is stiff, thin and disposable, so it's a standard improvised bookmark.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Photograph: A photograph is flat and sturdy, though the paper and chemicals can leave marks on pages in time.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Envelope: An envelope is flat and a handy size, and is good enough to hold a place for a long train ride.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Business card: A business card is sturdy, thin and always in your wallet, so many readers use one.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Sticky note: A sticky note's weak adhesive was an accident by 3M's Spencer Silver in 1968, and it won't harm pages.
Terrible things to use as a bookmark.Gift tag: A gift tag is small, stiff and often has a string, so it serves nicely as a bookmark.

Things in a police station.Jail cell: Short-term cells in stations usually hold people awaiting charge or court, while prisons house those already sentenced to long terms.
Things in a police station.Interrogation room: Many are fitted with a one-way mirror and recording gear, so a whole confession can later be reviewed by a court.
Things in a police station.Mugshot camera: The first systematic criminal photographs were taken in the 1840s, soon after photography itself was invented.
Things in a police station.Handcuffs: Modern double-locking cuffs have a pin that stops them tightening further, so they can't squeeze a wrist harder over time.
Things in a police station.Front desk: Most people's only contact with the police happens here, filing reports, asking for directions or collecting lost property.
Things in a police station.Squad car: Marked cars are often painted in high-contrast colors so they are recognized instantly, even from far down a street.
Things in a police station.Evidence locker: Evidence is logged with a chain of custody, and a gap in that record can get otherwise solid evidence thrown out of court.
Things in a police station.Fingerprint kit: Fingerprints stay unique even among identical twins, and a fine dusting powder makes the oily ridge pattern visible.
Things in a police station.Holding cell: Often just a bench and a toilet, it is meant for hours rather than days, until a suspect is released, charged or moved.
Things in a police station.Radio dispatcher: The dispatcher is the unseen hub of police work, hearing a call first and keeping officers aware of where backup is.
Things in a police station.Wanted posters: Posters like these were famous in the American West, but today's version is usually a photo shared online within minutes.
Things in a police station.Fire pole: Slides down from a firehouse's sleeping floor, saving seconds, so it belongs to a fire station, not a police station.
Things in a police station.Fire engine: It's the firefighters' ride, built to carry water, hose and ladders, so it belongs at the fire station down the road.
Things in a police station.Altar: Altars belong to places of worship; a police station deals with law and order, not ceremonies.
Things in a police station.Operating table: Surgeries take place in hospitals; a station's nearest equivalent is a first-aid kit and a call to paramedics.
Things in a police station.Pizza oven: Officers may love pizza, but ovens belong in kitchens, and the stereotype about police and donuts is the more famous snack myth.
Things in a police station.Dental chair: A dentist's tilting chair is built for long mouth examinations and has no place in a station, though a cell may feel as little fun.
Things in a police station.Hair salon: Salons are for styling, not law enforcement, though they are famously good places to hear neighborhood news.
Things in a police station.Bowling lane: A standard lane is about 18 meters from foul line to head pin, and none of that space is found in a station.
Things in a police station.Ball pit: Ball pits were invented in the 1970s and are for play areas, not police work, and they're a surprisingly hard place to find a lost phone.
Things in a police station.Hot tub: Warm soaks are for spas, not custody, and even the nicest holding cell has no jets.
Things in a police station.Jukebox: A jukebox belongs in a diner or bar, though in the 1950s a coin-fed machine was often considered a symbol of teenage rebellion.
Things in a police station.Pulpit: Preachers speak from a raised pulpit in a church, while police speak from a front desk or a press-conference podium.
Things in a police station.Slot machine: Slots belong in casinos, and in some places police do raid venues with illegal gaming machines.

Things a tailor uses.Thimble: A thimble protects the finger when pushing a needle through thick cloth, and some old ones were made of silver.
Things a tailor uses.Needle: Needles are among the oldest tools, and bone needles over 40,000 years old have been found.
Things a tailor uses.Thread: Thread is usually waxed or run through beeswax, which makes it stronger and keeps it from tangling.
Things a tailor uses.Tape measure: A tailor's tape is flexible and often marked in both inches and centimeters, and it was long a symbol of the trade.
Things a tailor uses.Pincushion: A pincushion keeps pins within reach, and many old ones were filled with sawdust or even human hair.
Things a tailor uses.Sewing machine: The first practical machines appeared in the 1840s and made sewing much faster than by hand.
Things a tailor uses.Pinking shears: Pinking shears cut a zigzag edge that keeps woven fabric from fraying, so they save on a finishing seam.
Things a tailor uses.Seam ripper: A seam ripper has a tiny blade and a ball tip to pick out stitches without cutting the cloth.
Things a tailor uses.Tailor's chalk: Tailors mark cloth with chalk because it brushes away and doesn't leave a stain.
Things a tailor uses.Bobbin: A bobbin holds the lower thread on a sewing machine, and the stitch is formed where the upper and lower threads lock.
Things a tailor uses.Dress form: A dress form is a torso mannequin that lets a tailor fit garments, and can be adjusted to a client's body.
Things a tailor uses.Chisel: A chisel is for carving, so it belongs to a carpenter or sculptor.
Things a tailor uses.Trowel: A trowel is for gardening or bricklaying and not for stitching.
Things a tailor uses.Whisk: A whisk is a kitchen tool for eggs and cream.
Things a tailor uses.Anvil: An anvil is a blacksmith's block, far too heavy for a tailor's shop.
Things a tailor uses.Kiln: A kiln is a potter's oven, hot enough to fire clay.
Things a tailor uses.Spatula: A spatula flips food, so it's for cooks.
Things a tailor uses.Wrench: A wrench turns bolts, which belongs in a mechanic's workshop.
Things a tailor uses.Easel: An easel holds a painter's canvas, not cloth.
Things a tailor uses.Loom: A loom weaves fabric, so it makes cloth, but a tailor then cuts and sews it.
Things a tailor uses.Spinning wheel: A spinning wheel makes thread, which is the stage before a tailor's work.
Things a tailor uses.Pitchfork: A pitchfork moves hay and has no use in making clothes.
Things a tailor uses.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is a doctor's tool and not for fitting suits.
Things a tailor uses.Plunger: A plunger unclogs sinks, a plumber's tool.

Things an electrician uses.Wire strippers: They remove insulation without nicking the copper, because each notch matches a specific wire gauge.
Things an electrician uses.Multimeter: It measures voltage, current and resistance, and careful electricians test it on a known live source first to be sure it works.
Things an electrician uses.Voltage tester: A pen-style tester beeps when it senses an AC field, so electricians can confirm a wire is dead before touching it.
Things an electrician uses.Electrical tape: Stretchy vinyl insulates a splice, and colored tape also marks wires or phases so circuits stay identifiable.
Things an electrician uses.Conduit: Metal or plastic tubes protect wiring from damage, and steel conduit can also help carry fault current to ground.
Things an electrician uses.Fish tape: A long flexible steel ribbon pushed through walls and conduit so that wires can be pulled along behind it.
Things an electrician uses.Insulated gloves: Rubber insulating gloves are rated for specific voltages and are air-tested for pinholes before use.
Things an electrician uses.Junction box: Every wire splice lives inside one, so connections stay protected and accessible instead of buried in a wall.
Things an electrician uses.Wire nuts: Twist-on connectors join wires with a metal spring inside a plastic cap, replacing the need to solder and tape each splice.
Things an electrician uses.Cable ties: The one-way toothed design was patented by Thomas and Betts in 1958 for aircraft wiring, and it only tightens.
Things an electrician uses.Circuit tester: A small lamp glows when a socket or wire is live, giving a quick check for power or continuity.
Things an electrician uses.Plunger: A plumber's rubber cup that works by suction, forcing water through a clogged drain.
Things an electrician uses.Pipe wrench: Its serrated jaws bite harder the more you pull, ideal for round pipes but a plumber's tool.
Things an electrician uses.Trowel: A bricklayer's and gardener's tool; the pointed blade spreads mortar, not wires.
Things an electrician uses.Whisk: Whisks work by stirring air into food, and a motor-driven kitchen version is just the same idea spun faster.
Things an electrician uses.Easel: Portable easels let the Impressionists paint outdoors, but they hold canvases, not cables.
Things an electrician uses.Scalpel: A surgeon's blade; the word comes from the Latin scalpere, to scratch or cut.
Things an electrician uses.Plumber's putty: A soft, clay-like seal for sinks and drains, easily mistaken for something an electrician might use.
Things an electrician uses.Drain snake: A coiled steel auger plumbers feed into a clog; it resembles fish tape, but the job is pipes, not wires.
Things an electrician uses.Pitchfork: Wooden handles do not make a pitchfork safe near power lines, since damp wood can conduct.
Things an electrician uses.Rolling pin: A baker's tool; some are marble and chilled so the pastry stays cool.
Things an electrician uses.Sickle: A curved hand blade for harvesting grain, one of the oldest farm tools and a symbol on the old Soviet flag.
Things an electrician uses.Thimble: A sewing thimble protects the fingertip, though riggers also use a metal cable thimble to protect wire rope loops.
Things an electrician uses.Bellows: A blacksmith's bellows pumps air into a fire to raise its temperature, which is the opposite of what an electrician wants.

Google products.Gmail: It launched on April 1, 2004, offering a gigabyte of storage when rivals gave a few megabytes, so many people thought it was a prank.
Google products.YouTube: Google bought it in 2006 for about 1.65 billion dollars, a year after the first video, Me at the zoo, was posted.
Google products.Android: Google bought the startup in 2005, and the system now runs on most of the world's smartphones.
Google products.Chrome: Launched in 2008 with a comic book explaining how it worked, and it's now the world's most-used browser.
Google products.Google Maps: It grew from a 2004 acquisition of Where 2 Technologies, and Street View followed in 2007.
Google products.Pixel: Google's own phone line since 2016, and its camera software is known for computational photography.
Google products.Google Drive: Launched in 2012, it gives cloud storage and the home for Docs, Sheets and Slides.
Google products.Nest: Google bought the smart-thermostat maker in 2014 for about 3.2 billion dollars.
Google products.Waze: Google bought the Israeli community-driven traffic app in 2013 for about a billion dollars or more.
Google products.Fitbit: Founded in 2007, the fitness tracker maker was acquired by Google in 2021 for about 2.1 billion dollars.
Google products.Gemini: Google's AI model family, which carries the name of the twin constellation and succeeded its earlier Bard chatbot.
Google products.Bing: Microsoft's search engine, the main competitor to Google, not one of its products.
Google products.Safari: Apple's browser, even though Google pays billions to be its default search engine.
Google products.Outlook: Microsoft's email, which competes with Gmail.
Google products.Alexa: Amazon's voice assistant, first on the Echo in 2014, a rival to Google Assistant.
Google products.Siri: Apple's voice assistant arrived on the iPhone 4S in 2011, and it began as a separate startup.
Google products.Kindle: Amazon's e-reader, launched in 2007, not made by Google.
Google products.Instagram: Owned by Meta and bought in 2012, so it's not a Google product.
Google products.WhatsApp: Meta bought it in 2014 for about 19 billion dollars, and it's not Google's.
Google products.Firefox: Mozilla's browser, an independent rival to Chrome that has existed since 2004.
Google products.Excel: Microsoft's spreadsheet, whereas Google's equivalent is Sheets.
Google products.Zoom: A separate company's video meeting software; Google's equivalent is Meet.
Google products.Slack: A work chat app whose name stands for Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge, and it now belongs to Salesforce.
Google products.Spotify: A Swedish music streaming service, rather than a Google product; Google's own is YouTube Music.

Star Wars technology.Lightsaber: Its sound mixes a film projector's hum with the buzz of a CRT TV, created by sound designer Ben Burtt.
Star Wars technology.Droid: R2-D2's beeps were made by Burtt with a synthesizer and his own voice.
Star Wars technology.Hyperdrive: It jumps to lightspeed, and Han claims the Falcon made the Kessel Run in under twelve parsecs, a unit of distance.
Star Wars technology.Blaster: Burtt created the blaster sound by hitting a radio tower's guy-wire.
Star Wars technology.Death Star: A moon-sized battle station with a superlaser, destroyed because of a fatal flaw in its thermal exhaust port design.
Star Wars technology.Holocron: An ancient data cube holding knowledge of the Jedi or the Sith.
Star Wars technology.X-wing: The Rebel starfighter whose wings open into attack position.
Star Wars technology.TIE Fighter: TIE stands for Twin Ion Engine, and its roar combined an elephant call and a car on a wet road.
Star Wars technology.Millennium Falcon: Han Solo's ship, which Lucas reportedly said was inspired by a hamburger with an olive beside it.
Star Wars technology.Speeder bike: The Endor chase was filmed by walking a camera through a redwood forest and speeding up the footage.
Star Wars technology.AT-AT: The Empire Strikes Back's walkers were brought to life through stop-motion animation of small models.
Star Wars technology.Carbonite: It freezes Han Solo in Empire, and the name riffs on the real element carbon.
Star Wars technology.Thermal detonator: A small bomb that Leia, disguised as Boushh, threatens to use in Return of the Jedi.
Star Wars technology.Phaser: A trap: Star Trek's handheld energy weapon, with stun settings.
Star Wars technology.Tricorder: Star Trek's scanning gadget, which inspired real handheld medical scanners.
Star Wars technology.Transporter: Star Trek's beaming device, created because the budget couldn't afford landing a shuttle every week.
Star Wars technology.Warp drive: Star Trek's faster-than-light engine; physicist Miguel Alcubierre proposed a theoretical version in 1994.
Star Wars technology.Holodeck: Star Trek's room that creates virtual worlds from The Next Generation.
Star Wars technology.Replicator: Star Trek's food maker, famous for Tea, Earl Grey, hot.
Star Wars technology.USS Enterprise: Star Trek's flagship, named after real ships and echoed by the first space shuttle after a fan campaign.
Star Wars technology.Borg Cube: Star Trek's cube-shaped ships belonging to the Borg.
Star Wars technology.Communicator: Star Trek's flip device that inspired the flip phone; Martin Cooper cited it.
Star Wars technology.Photon torpedo: Star Trek's explosive antimatter weapon, fired from starships; Star Wars uses proton torpedoes instead.
Star Wars technology.Bat'leth: A Klingon curved sword from Star Trek, not Star Wars.
