Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Amazon: It began in 1994 as a bookstore in Jeff Bezos's garage, and now a large share of its sales come from third-party sellers.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Etsy: Founded in 2005 in Brooklyn, it specializes in handmade, vintage and craft supplies, and its name was reportedly inspired by Italian speech.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Craigslist: Craig Newmark started it in 1995 as an email list of San Francisco events, and it has barely changed its plain look since.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Alibaba: Jack Ma founded it in 1999 in his apartment, and its name was chosen because people everywhere recognize Ali Baba.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.AliExpress: This Alibaba-owned site sells directly from Chinese sellers to buyers worldwide, often with shipping times of several weeks.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Depop: This London-born app turned secondhand fashion into a social feed, and it is especially popular with Gen Z shoppers.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Poshmark: Its users host live shopping parties, and sellers get their items shared across the app's social feed.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Mercari: This Japanese flea-market app grew huge at home before it expanded into the US, where it popularized quick sell-from-your-phone listings.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Vinted: This Lithuanian marketplace for secondhand clothes charges buyers rather than sellers, which is unusual for resale apps.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.OfferUp: This US app focuses on local pickup, and it has featured safe-meetup spots to make strangers' swaps feel less risky.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Temu: Launched in 2022 by PDD Holdings, it shot up app-store charts thanks to extremely low prices and a huge advertising spend.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Netflix: It started in 1997 mailing DVDs and only later streamed; it makes content rather than connecting buyers and sellers.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Spotify: The Swedish service sells subscriptions to music it licenses, so it is a store of one company, not a marketplace.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Wikipedia: This free encyclopedia is written by volunteers and sells nothing, with no ads either.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Reddit: It has communities for buying and selling, like r/mechmarket, but the site itself is a forum, not a store.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Google Maps: It shows businesses and routes, but the sale itself happens elsewhere, since Maps does not host listings from sellers.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Zoom: Video calls here grew from about 10 million daily meeting participants in late 2019 to over 300 million by April 2020.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Duolingo: Its green owl mascot is known for guilt-tripping learners with reminders, and the app sells subscriptions, not goods from other people.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Waze: Google bought this community-driven navigation app in 2013 for about a billion dollars, and drivers report hazards in real time.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Shazam: It identifies songs from a few seconds of audio, and Apple bought it in 2018.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Gmail: Launched on April 1, 2004, many people thought its one gigabyte of free storage was a joke.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Slack: Its name is an acronym for Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge, and it began as a game company's internal tool.
Online marketplaces for buying and selli.Tinder: It sells matches rather than goods, and its swipe gesture became a model for countless apps.

Games from Rockstar Games.Grand Theft Auto: GTA V has sold over 200 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games ever, and earned billions in revenue.
Games from Rockstar Games.Red Dead Redemption: The 2010 western became famous for its horseback open world and a bittersweet ending players still debate.
Games from Rockstar Games.Max Payne: Made by Finland's Remedy, whose 2001 game pioneered bullet time in shooters; Rockstar later bought the rights and made Max Payne 3.
Games from Rockstar Games.Bully: Released in 2006 (as Canis Canem Edit in Europe), it set a prankster teen loose in a boarding school and drew controversy before launch.
Games from Rockstar Games.L.A. Noire: Team Bondi's 1940s detective game used a facial-capture system with dozens of cameras to record actors' expressions.
Games from Rockstar Games.Midnight Club: Rockstar San Diego's street-racing series let you drive through open cities, with no set tracks.
Games from Rockstar Games.Manhunt: This 2003 stealth horror game was banned in some countries for violence and became a major censorship story.
Games from Rockstar Games.The Warriors: Rockstar's 2005 brawler adapted the 1979 cult film about a New York gang trying to cross the city after a false accusation.
Games from Rockstar Games.Smuggler's Run: A 2000 PS2 launch-era title about smuggling contraband across open terrain, which showed off the new console's physics.
Games from Rockstar Games.Red Dead Revolver: The 2004 western began life at Capcom; Rockstar took over and released it, planting the seed for Red Dead Redemption.
Games from Rockstar Games.Saints Row: Volition's series began as a GTA rival, then veered into increasingly absurd comedy. It's not a Rockstar game.
Games from Rockstar Games.Mafia: Made by Czech studio Illusion Softworks and now owned by 2K, it is often compared to GTA but isn't from Rockstar.
Games from Rockstar Games.Watch Dogs: Ubisoft's hacking-themed open-world game from 2014. A GTA lookalike in format, but not Rockstar's.
Games from Rockstar Games.Sleeping Dogs: An open-world Hong Kong crime game from Square Enix's studio, not Rockstar; it began as an Activision project.
Games from Rockstar Games.Just Cause: Avalanche Studios' series is famous for grappling hooks and absurd explosions, and was never a Rockstar title.
Games from Rockstar Games.Far Cry: Ubisoft's open-world shooter series, which began as a tech demo by Crytek; no Rockstar link.
Games from Rockstar Games.Assassin's Creed: Ubisoft's historical stealth series. It looks like a Rockstar-style open world but belongs to a different publisher.
Games from Rockstar Games.The Witcher: CD Projekt Red's fantasy RPG, based on Polish books by Andrzej Sapkowski, not a Rockstar game.
Games from Rockstar Games.Cyberpunk 2077: CD Projekt's 2020 release had a notoriously rough launch; it's an RPG from Poland, not a Rockstar title.
Games from Rockstar Games.Halo: Microsoft's Xbox flagship, from Bungie and later 343 Industries. It's a sci-fi shooter, not Rockstar.
Games from Rockstar Games.Fallout: Bethesda's post-apocalyptic RPG series, set in a retro-futuristic 1950s world. No Rockstar involvement.
Games from Rockstar Games.Skyrim: Bethesda's 2011 fantasy epic has been re-released on dozens of platforms, but is not a Rockstar game.
Games from Rockstar Games.Hitman: IO Interactive's assassin series stars Agent 47, with a famously bald head and barcode tattoo; not from Rockstar.
Games from Rockstar Games.Driver: Ubisoft's Reflections series, which began in 1999, is an easy mix-up with GTA's car chases, but Rockstar didn't make it.

Mobile phone operating systems.iOS: Introduced in 2007 as iPhone OS, it was renamed iOS in 2010 and runs all iPhones.
Mobile phone operating systems.Android: Android Inc. began as a camera OS before Google bought it in 2005; today it runs on most smartphones in the world.
Mobile phone operating systems.Windows Phone: Microsoft's mobile OS replaced Windows Mobile in 2010 and was eventually abandoned, with support ending in 2019.
Mobile phone operating systems.BlackBerry OS: Once the business favorite for phones with physical keyboards; it was largely replaced by BlackBerry 10 and then Android.
Mobile phone operating systems.Symbian: Nokia's main phone OS for years; it was once the world's most-used smartphone platform before iOS and Android took over.
Mobile phone operating systems.webOS: Palm's 2009 mobile OS, later bought by HP and then LG, which put it on smart TVs, where it lives on.
Mobile phone operating systems.Firefox OS: Mozilla's web-based phone OS aimed at low-cost phones, launched in 2013 and discontinued in 2016.
Mobile phone operating systems.Tizen: A Linux-based OS led by Samsung, now mostly found on its smart TVs and watches.
Mobile phone operating systems.HarmonyOS: Huawei's operating system, created after US sanctions cut its access to Google's Android services.
Mobile phone operating systems.Palm OS: Created for the Palm Pilot in 1996, it was an early PDA system and ancestor of the smartphone.
Mobile phone operating systems.macOS: The Mac desktop operating system. Despite sharing a heritage with iOS, it doesn't run on phones.
Mobile phone operating systems.Windows 95: A landmark desktop OS that introduced the Start button in 1995; it never ran on phones.
Mobile phone operating systems.MS-DOS: Microsoft's command-line OS for IBM PCs, from 1981, which predated all smartphones by decades.
Mobile phone operating systems.ChromeOS: Google's OS for Chromebooks is browser-centric and for laptops and desktops, not phones.
Mobile phone operating systems.Solaris: Sun Microsystems' Unix OS, aimed at servers and workstations, not phones.
Mobile phone operating systems.FreeBSD: A Unix-like OS for servers, and parts of it live inside Apple's systems and PlayStation consoles, but it's not a phone OS.
Mobile phone operating systems.Windows XP: Released in 2001, it ran on desktops and laptops and remained widely used for years.
Mobile phone operating systems.Windows Vista: Released in 2007 to a mixed reception, it was a desktop OS, not a phone system.
Mobile phone operating systems.OS/2: IBM and Microsoft jointly started it for PCs in the 1980s, but they later split ways.
Mobile phone operating systems.Mac OS X: Apple's 2001 desktop OS was built on Unix, and its later name, macOS, is still for computers, not phones.
Mobile phone operating systems.Fedora: A community Linux distribution sponsored by Red Hat, used on desktops and servers; the name comes from a hat logo.
Mobile phone operating systems.AmigaOS: The OS of the Commodore Amiga, known for early multitasking in 1985; it was a computer OS.
Mobile phone operating systems.Debian: A widely used Linux distribution created in 1993 and the base for Ubuntu, but not a phone OS.
Mobile phone operating systems.Unix: Created at Bell Labs in the 1970s, it's the ancestor of many systems, but is a general-purpose OS not specific to phones.

Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Aladdin: Not in the oldest Arabic manuscripts; French translator Antoine Galland added the tale in the early 1700s after hearing it from storyteller Hanna Diyab.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Ali Baba: "Open Sesame" opens the thieves' cave; sesame pods burst open when ripe, a possible origin for the magic phrase. He came via Galland, too.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Sinbad: His seven voyages feature giant birds, a whale mistaken for an island and the Old Man of the Sea riding on his back.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Scheherazade: She tells stories each night to delay her execution, stopping at dawn on cliffhangers; she survives all 1,001 nights.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Shahryar: The king who executes each bride after the wedding night until Scheherazade's tales cure him.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.The Genie: The word comes from the jinn of Islamic tradition, beings made of smokeless fire; Galland chose "génie" for how it sounds like "genius".
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Morgiana: The clever slave girl who saves Ali Baba's family and kills the forty thieves by pouring boiling oil into the jars they hide in.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Cassim: Ali Baba's greedy brother forgets the magic word to open the cave and is caught and killed by the thieves.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Dunyazad: Scheherazade's younger sister who asks her to tell a story each night so that the king will stay awake and listen.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Harun al-Rashid: A real caliph who ruled the Abbasid Empire from Baghdad from 786 to 809; the tales often show him wandering the city in disguise.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Abu: Aladdin's monkey sidekick exists only in Disney's 1992 film; the original tale has no such pet, just a magician and a lamp.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Rajah: Princess Jasmine's pet tiger is Disney's invention, as is Jasmine's name in the form we know; the original princess is Badroulbadour.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Hercules: The strongman of Greek myth with his twelve labors; his stories are Greek, not part of the Arabian tale collection.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Odysseus: Homer's wily Greek hero spent ten years sailing home from Troy; his adventures are Greek epic, not part of the Nights.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Gilgamesh: The Mesopotamian king of Uruk is hero of a 4,000-year-old epic, far older than the Nights and from a different tradition.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Beowulf: Beowulf fights Grendel in an Old English poem, probably composed about a thousand years ago, set in Scandinavia.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Robin Hood: England's outlaw of Sherwood Forest, who robbed from the rich, is an English ballad hero, not an Arabian one.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Pinocchio: Carlo Collodi's wooden boy, whose nose grows when he lies, comes from an 1883 Italian novel.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Mowgli: Kipling's wolf-raised boy lives in the Indian jungle of The Jungle Book (1894), not in the world of the Nights.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Rumpelstiltskin: The Grimms' spinning imp who wants a firstborn child is a German tale, and he loses once his name is guessed.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Gulliver: Swift's Gulliver sails to Lilliput in a satire from 1726, written in English and no part of the Nights.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Baron Munchausen: Rudolf Erich Raspe's tall-tale baron, who rides a cannonball, was based on a real German nobleman and appeared in 1785.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.Ozymandias: Shelley's 1818 sonnet imagines a ruined statue of the pharaoh Ramesses II in the desert; no part of the Nights.
Characters in One Thousand and One Night.King Arthur: Arthur and his Round Table belong to British and Celtic legend, with Camelot and Excalibur, nothing from Baghdad.

Things in Hamlet.Skull: In the graveyard Hamlet holds the skull of Yorick, the king's jester, and muses 'Alas, poor Yorick!'; it is the most iconic prop in theater.
Things in Hamlet.Ghost: The ghost of Hamlet's father opens the play on the battlements and tells his son he was murdered by his brother.
Things in Hamlet.Poisoned blade: Laertes tips his sword with poison for the duel, and it ends up killing both Hamlet and Laertes himself.
Things in Hamlet.Poisoned cup: Claudius prepares a poisoned drink for Hamlet, but Queen Gertrude drinks it by mistake.
Things in Hamlet.Play within a play: Hamlet has actors stage 'The Murder of Gonzago' to catch the king's guilty reaction; he calls it 'The Mousetrap'.
Things in Hamlet.Graveyard: Act 5's graveyard scene brings Hamlet face to face with death, and with Ophelia's grave.
Things in Hamlet.Elsinore: Hamlet's castle is a real Danish fortress, Kronborg, in the town of Helsingør.
Things in Hamlet.Duel: Hamlet and Laertes fence in the climactic duel, which turns deadly through a poisoned sword and drink.
Things in Hamlet.Gravedigger: The comic gravedigger trades jokes with Hamlet, and is one of Shakespeare's most celebrated clowns.
Things in Hamlet.Pirates: Hamlet's ship is boarded by pirates on the way to England, and they return him to Denmark.
Things in Hamlet.Denmark: Hamlet gave us 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark', where the entire play unfolds.
Things in Hamlet.Recorder: Hamlet uses a recorder to show Guildenstern that he can't be 'played upon' like an instrument.
Things in Hamlet.Witches: The witches belong to Macbeth, not Hamlet.
Things in Hamlet.Cauldron: The cauldron bubbles in Macbeth's witches' scene.
Things in Hamlet.Balcony: The balcony belongs to Romeo and Juliet; Hamlet's key spots are the castle battlements, where the ghost appears, and the graveyard.
Things in Hamlet.Handkerchief: The handkerchief is Othello's token of suspected love.
Things in Hamlet.Shipwreck: The Tempest begins with a shipwreck; Hamlet has pirates, but no wreck.
Things in Hamlet.Pound of flesh: Shylock's demand comes from The Merchant of Venice.
Things in Hamlet.Love potion: Love potions are Puck's trick in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Things in Hamlet.Donkey's head: Bottom wears the donkey's head in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Things in Hamlet.Birnam Wood: The marching wood belongs to Macbeth, whose doom comes when Birnam Wood seems to move toward Dunsinane Castle.
Things in Hamlet.Three caskets: The three caskets are in The Merchant of Venice.
Things in Hamlet.Masquerade ball: The masked ball belongs to Romeo and Juliet.
Things in Hamlet.Sleepwalking: Sleepwalking is Lady Macbeth's habit; in Hamlet it is Ophelia who goes mad, not sleepwalks.

Things you can put in a compost bin.Banana peel: Banana peels break down quickly and add potassium to compost, though in open air they can take weeks to vanish fully.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Coffee grounds: Used coffee grounds are rich in nitrogen, so composters count them as a green material despite their brown color.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Eggshells: Crushed eggshells add calcium to compost, but they break down slowly, so grinding them fine helps a lot.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Apple core: Apple cores compost happily, and the seeds inside might even sprout in your heap, though they rarely grow true to the parent fruit.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Grass clippings: Fresh clippings heat a pile up fast because they're nitrogen-rich, but a thick layer can turn slimy and smelly without brown material mixed in.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Fallen leaves: Autumn leaves are the classic carbon-rich brown material, and shredded leaves can turn into crumbly leaf mold within a year or two.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Tea leaves: Loose tea leaves compost easily. Check tea bags first, since some contain a little plastic that won't break down.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Carrot peels: Carrot peels are quick to break down, and chopping scraps small speeds up any compost pile.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Shredded newspaper: Newsprint is mostly paper and compostable, and modern inks are often soy-based, so shredded paper works as a brown layer.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Wood chips: Wood chips are slow, carbon-rich bulk that keeps a pile airy, and they take far longer to rot than kitchen scraps.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Sawdust: Sawdust is a great carbon source but only from untreated wood, since chemicals in treated lumber can end up in your soil.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Cardboard: Plain cardboard composts well when torn up, though shiny or heavily printed boxes are better avoided.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Plastic bag: A plastic bag can linger for hundreds of years; even so-called biodegradable ones often need industrial composting, not a backyard bin.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Glass bottle: Glass is made from sand and can be recycled endlessly, but it never breaks down in a compost heap.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Aluminum can: Recycling aluminum saves roughly 95 percent of the energy needed to make it fresh, but it doesn't belong in compost.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Styrofoam: Foam packing is mostly air, up to about 98 percent, yet the polystyrene around it can persist for centuries instead of rotting.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Batteries: Batteries hold metals and chemicals like lead or cadmium that would poison compost, so they belong at a special drop-off.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Metal fork: Metal won't rot in a compost bin, so a fork thrown in by mistake will come out unchanged, along with your finished soil.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Bubble wrap: Bubble wrap began in 1957 as an attempted textured wallpaper; as plastic, it won't ever compost.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Nylon sock: Nylon is a synthetic plastic invented in the 1930s, so a nylon sock will sit in a compost pile almost unchanged for decades.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Plastic straw: A plastic straw can take hundreds of years to break down, which is partly why many places have banned them.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Light bulb: Compact fluorescent bulbs contain a little mercury, so bulbs of any kind need proper disposal and never go in compost.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Chip bag: Chip bags are shiny multilayer plastic and foil laminates that make them very hard to recycle or compost.
Things you can put in a compost bin.Crayon: Crayons are made from paraffin wax, a petroleum product, so they won't break down in a compost heap.

Parts of a theatre.Stage: Upstage means toward the back because old stages sloped upward away from the audience, forcing actors downstage to move closer.
Parts of a theatre.Curtain: Many theatres still have a fireproof safety curtain, a legacy of 19th-century auditorium fires that killed hundreds.
Parts of a theatre.Box office: The name dates from when private boxes were sold at this window, and it now also describes how much a film earns.
Parts of a theatre.Orchestra pit: Wagner's Bayreuth theatre hid the orchestra in a covered pit so the audience would see only the drama, not the musicians.
Parts of a theatre.Balcony: In British theatres the highest, cheapest seats were nicknamed 'the gods' because of their lofty position and the ceiling paintings above them.
Parts of a theatre.Dressing room: Those bulb-ringed mirrors exist for honesty: strong even light shows actors exactly how their stage makeup will look.
Parts of a theatre.Wings: Actors who stand ready offstage are 'waiting in the wings', and that phrase became a common idiom for anyone prepared to step in.
Parts of a theatre.Spotlight: Before electric light, stages used burning limes for a brilliant glow, which is why we still say 'in the limelight'.
Parts of a theatre.Backdrop: Early stagehands were often ex-sailors because rigging scenery on ropes in the fly tower needed their skills, and they brought nautical terms along.
Parts of a theatre.Trapdoor: Elizabethan stages had a trap, and the space beneath was called 'hell', ideal for ghosts and devils who vanished in a puff.
Parts of a theatre.Footlights: Gas-lit footlights were a notorious fire hazard, and 'the footlights' became shorthand for the stage and for performing itself.
Parts of a theatre.Green room: Nobody is certain why it is called green, and the lounge is rarely painted that color. It is where performers wait before their cue.
Parts of a theatre.Proscenium: The word comes from Greek for 'in front of the scene', and the arch frames the stage like a picture to separate actors and audience.
Parts of a theatre.Dugout: Dugouts are sunk below field level in baseball so the crowd's view is not blocked. They shelter players, not actors.
Parts of a theatre.Bullpen: Relief pitchers warm up in the bullpen. It sounds backstage, but it is baseball, and nobody agrees on the origin of the name.
Parts of a theatre.Pit lane: The pit lane is where Formula 1 teams change tyres in about two seconds. 'Pit' fits, but this is racing, not theatre.
Parts of a theatre.Cockpit: A cockpit is the pilot's compartment, but the word first named an arena for cockfights, nothing to do with plays.
Parts of a theatre.Engine room: The engine room is a ship's machinery space. It is loud, hot and backstage-like, but it is nautical, not theatrical.
Parts of a theatre.Hayloft: A hayloft is a barn's upper storage floor. It is a loft above, but not the sort a theatre has.
Parts of a theatre.Bank vault: Bank vaults guard cash, and some are so thick that opening them takes timers. A theatre's own money sits in the box office instead.
Parts of a theatre.Penalty box: The penalty box is where ice hockey players serve minor penalties of two minutes, nothing to do with a theatre.
Parts of a theatre.Altar: The altar is the church table for communion. Theatres sometimes get called temples of drama, but they have no altar.
Parts of a theatre.Pulpit: A pulpit is a raised church platform for sermons, and the classic Moby-Dick one has a rope ladder, but theatres have a stage instead.
Parts of a theatre.Jury box: The jury box seats a court's jurors, usually twelve. It is a courtroom seat, not a theatre one.

Words that go before 'house'.Light: Lighthouse keepers once trimmed wicks and polished lenses; the Fresnel lens, invented in 1822, let beams reach well over 20 miles.
Words that go before 'house'.Green: A greenhouse works by trapping warmth as sunlight passes through glass but heat inside can't easily escape.
Words that go before 'house'.Ware: Warehouse comes from 'ware', meaning goods for sale; the same root appears in hardware and software.
Words that go before 'house'.Club: Clubhouse originally meant a building owned by a social club, and it's now most familiar at golf courses and sports grounds.
Words that go before 'house'.Court: A courthouse is where legal cases are heard; the word 'court' once also meant a king's household and followers.
Words that go before 'house'.Opera: The Sydney Opera House took 14 years to build instead of the 4 planned, and cost about 14 times the original budget.
Words that go before 'house'.Farm: Farmhouse describes the main dwelling on a farm, and the word 'farm' started as a fixed rent payment, not a place.
Words that go before 'house'.Dog: Being 'in the doghouse' means being in trouble, and it's often linked to the dog kennel in Peter Pan, where Mr. Darling lives out of shame.
Words that go before 'house'.Boat: Houseboats are lived in on rivers and canals; Kashmir's Dal Lake famously has floating wooden ones with carved interiors.
Words that go before 'house'.Tree: A treehouse is built on or around a tree trunk, and some are strong enough that people have lived in them for years.
Words that go before 'house'.Hen: A henhouse is a coop for chickens; the saying 'fox in the henhouse' refers to a predator who is somewhere he can do harm.
Words that go before 'house'.Guest: A guesthouse is a small lodging place, often a separate building on the owner's property, as well as a type of budget hotel.
Words that go before 'house'.Doll: Dollhouses date back to 16th-century Europe, when wealthy adults commissioned elaborate cabinet versions of their own homes.
Words that go before 'house'.Nursing: 'Nursing house' isn't a standard compound; the usual term is nursing home, which is the trap.
Words that go before 'house'.Mobile: Mobile home is the standard phrase; 'mobile house' is not a common compound word in everyday English.
Words that go before 'house'.Care: Care home is the usual expression for residential care, so 'care house' isn't a normal word.
Words that go before 'house'.Igloo: Igloo is itself a kind of house, built of snow blocks, so 'igloo house' would be redundant rather than a word.
Words that go before 'house'.Hut: A hut is a small basic shelter, and people don't say 'hut house'; it's another type of building, not a prefix.
Words that go before 'house'.Palace: A palace is a grand residence, not something placed in front of 'house' to form a compound.
Words that go before 'house'.Hotel: Hotel is a type of lodging, but no one says 'hotel house'; people say 'house hotel' only rarely.
Words that go before 'house'.Cabin: 'Cabin house' isn't a standard phrase; a log cabin is already a small house, and nobody uses it as a prefix.
Words that go before 'house'.Garage: A garage is part of many houses but 'garage house' isn't a standard compound; you'd say 'house garage'.
Words that go before 'house'.Nest: A nest is a bird's home, but 'nest house' isn't an English compound, however home-like it feels.
Words that go before 'house'.Kennel: A kennel is already a dog's house, so 'kennel house' makes little sense, unlike 'doghouse'.

Things in a post office.Stamps: The Penny Black of 1840, Britain's first adhesive postage stamp, made the sender pay rather than the recipient.
Things in a post office.Envelope: Early envelopes were folded by hand; the machine to make them came in the mid-1800s, and the gummed flap soon followed.
Things in a post office.Parcel: Parcel post reached the US in 1913, and a few parents famously mailed small children cheaply until the Post Office banned it.
Things in a post office.Scale: Post office scales weigh parcels because postage is based on weight and size, so a gram can change the price.
Things in a post office.Counter: Counter service has shrunk as letters declined, but the boom in online shopping keeps parcel counters busy.
Things in a post office.Mailbag: Mail trains once snatched bags from trackside hooks without stopping, using catcher arms, so letters sped on overnight.
Things in a post office.PO box: PO boxes let people receive mail without a street address, and they remain popular with businesses and people who move often.
Things in a post office.Postmark: A postmark proves when and where a letter was posted, and collectors prize old ones on stamps and envelopes.
Things in a post office.Postcard: Postcards boomed around 1900, when with several deliveries a day people used them like text messages.
Things in a post office.Postal clerk: Sorting mail on moving trains was once a skilled job: railway post office clerks could memorize thousands of destinations.
Things in a post office.Bubble wrap: Bubble wrap began as 1950s textured wallpaper, and only later turned out to be great for packing.
Things in a post office.Stethoscope: A stethoscope listens to the heart and lungs, so it belongs in a clinic, not a post office.
Things in a post office.Gavel: A gavel belongs to judges and auctioneers, who both bang to end things; postal workers just use a stamp.
Things in a post office.Saddle: A saddle goes on a horse; the Pony Express riders carried the mail on one, but a post office doesn't stock them.
Things in a post office.Trapeze: A trapeze swings in the circus tent; a post office has no need for acrobats, however acrobatic the Christmas rush gets.
Things in a post office.Cauldron: A cauldron is for witches and stews, not stamps and parcels.
Things in a post office.Easel: An easel props a canvas for a painter, so it fits an art studio, not a postal hall.
Things in a post office.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is a hay-moving tool, not postal stock, though 'Grant Wood's American Gothic' made one famous.
Things in a post office.Fishing rod: A fishing rod is for angling, and in a post office the only 'tackle' is sticky tape.
Things in a post office.Kayak: The kayak is an Inuit invention thousands of years old, a hunting craft rather than anything for the mail counter.
Things in a post office.Barbell: A barbell is a gym item, even if a postal worker hauls heavy sacks all day.
Things in a post office.Ski poles: Ski poles help skiers push off and balance, so they're sports shop stock, not post office stock.
Things in a post office.Hay bale: Hay bales are farm fodder, not post office stock, though rural carriers do deliver to farm mailboxes.
Things in a post office.Snorkel: A snorkel lets you breathe while swimming face-down, which suits a pool, not a postal counter.

Hogwarts professors.Dumbledore: Albus Dumbledore's first name comes from the Latin for white, and he is the only headmaster to have beaten the dark wizard Grindelwald.
Hogwarts professors.McGonagall: Minerva McGonagall can turn into a tabby cat, with markings around her eyes that match her spectacles, and she taught Transfiguration for decades.
Hogwarts professors.Snape: Severus Snape taught Potions for years while longing for the Defence Against the Dark Arts job, which he finally got in book six.
Hogwarts professors.Flitwick: Tiny Filius Flitwick teaches Charms and heads Ravenclaw house; he was a dueling champion in his youth.
Hogwarts professors.Sprout: Pomona Sprout teaches Herbology and heads Hufflepuff; her mandrakes are what cure the petrified students in the second book.
Hogwarts professors.Lupin: Remus Lupin taught Defence Against the Dark Arts for one year, then resigned when his werewolf secret slipped out.
Hogwarts professors.Slughorn: Horace Slughorn collects talented or well-connected students into his Slug Club, and holds the Potions post twice.
Hogwarts professors.Trelawney: Sybill Trelawney teaches Divination, mostly by bluffing, yet she delivered two genuine prophecies, including the one about Harry and Voldemort.
Hogwarts professors.Quirrell: Quirinus Quirrell's turban hid Voldemort's face on the back of his head, making him the series' first secret villain at Hogwarts.
Hogwarts professors.Lockhart: Gilderoy Lockhart was a celebrity author who took credit for other wizards' deeds, then wiped their memories with Obliviate.
Hogwarts professors.Umbridge: Dolores Umbridge, a Ministry official, became Hogwarts High Inquisitor and punished students with a blood quill that carved words into their hands.
Hogwarts professors.Binns: Professor Binns teaches History of Magic, and is a ghost who simply stood up from his body one day and carried on teaching.
Hogwarts professors.Hagrid: Rubeus Hagrid was expelled as a student, yet came back as Keeper of Keys and later taught Care of Magical Creatures. He is half giant.
Hogwarts professors.Firenze: Firenze is a centaur who took over Divination, even though his herd banished him for helping humans.
Hogwarts professors.Filch: Argus Filch is the caretaker, not a professor; as a Squib, he is born to wizards but cannot do magic himself.
Hogwarts professors.Sirius Black: Sirius Black was a Hogwarts student, never a teacher; he is Harry's godfather and can turn into a big black dog.
Hogwarts professors.Voldemort: As Tom Riddle he asked Dumbledore for the Defence Against the Dark Arts job and was refused, never teaching there.
Hogwarts professors.Cornelius Fudge: Fudge was Minister for Magic, not a teacher, and stubbornly denied Voldemort's return for a long time.
Hogwarts professors.Lucius Malfoy: Lucius Malfoy sat on the school's board of governors and pressured them to oust Dumbledore, but he never taught a class.
Hogwarts professors.Dobby: Dobby works in the Hogwarts kitchens later on, but he is a house-elf, not a professor; a sock set him free.
Hogwarts professors.Bellatrix: Bellatrix Lestrange is a Death Eater and Sirius Black's cousin; her lessons were strictly Unforgivable Curses outside school.
Hogwarts professors.Arthur Weasley: Arthur Weasley works at the Ministry's Misuse of Muggle Artefacts office and loves rubber ducks and plugs, but doesn't teach.
Hogwarts professors.Ollivander: Garrick Ollivander sells wands in Diagon Alley and insists that the wand chooses the wizard; he is no professor.
Hogwarts professors.Rita Skeeter: Rita Skeeter is a gossip reporter who can secretly turn into a beetle to eavesdrop; she never taught at Hogwarts.

Famous romantic couples.Romeo & Juliet: Shakespeare's teenage lovers from feuding Verona families die within days of meeting; Juliet is nearly 14 in the play.
Famous romantic couples.Antony & Cleopatra: The Roman general and Egypt's queen were allies and lovers, and both took their own lives after losing to Octavian in 30 BC.
Famous romantic couples.Tristan & Isolde: A medieval legend of a Cornish knight and an Irish princess bound by a love potion; Wagner's opera of it premiered in 1865.
